translationRepairs: Li Kui's program quantified agricultural output gains from intensified cultivation within a calibrated land-assessment framework.
Serving Marquis Wen of Wei, Li Kui devised a program that quantified agricultural gains from more intensive cultivation within a calibrated assessment of available land.
李悝為魏文侯作盡地力之教 names Marquis Wen as Li Kui's patron. This revision restores that relationship while avoiding the proposal's awkward 'working for ... made a program' construction.
At thirty shi valued as 1,350 cash; removing village and sacrificial expenses of 300 cash leaves 1,050.
At thirty cash per shi, this is 1,350 cash; removing village and sacrificial expenses of 300 cash leaves 1,050.
Preceding surplus is forty-five shi; 石三十 at 1,350 cash is thirty cash per shi (45×30), not 'thirty shi valued as' that amount.
Reserve-release volumes should scale with famine severity: 100, 70, then 30 shi.
In a minor famine the harvest is about one hundred shi; in a moderate famine, seventy; in a major famine, thirty.
In context after bumper/middling/poor-year yield figures, 小飢則收百石 continues harvest-yield arithmetic; 'reserve-release volumes' invents the later 發斂 policy and the proposed harvest reading is correct.
Shang Yang's reforms were anti-classical but materially effective: they concentrated agrarian output and military mobilization.

When Duke Xiao of Qin employed Lord Shang, Shang Yang abolished the well-field system, opened the field boundaries, and offered urgent rewards for farming and war. Though these measures departed from ancient ways, their focus on fundamentals enabled Qin to overwhelm its neighbors and dominate the other lords.
秦孝公用商君 names Duke Xiao as patron and Lord Shang as reformer. This revision restores both and removes the proposal's ambiguous pronoun while retaining the reforms and their stated result.
Qin unification paired massive extraction and labor mobilization with frontier militarization and megaprojects.
Under the First Emperor, who annexed the realm, Qin paired massive extraction and labor mobilization with frontier militarization and megaprojects.
Omitting 始皇 is a real error, but 'By the First Emperor, Qin unification paired…' is awkward and underplays 遂并天下; name the emperor as annexing agent while keeping the rest of the accurate paraphrase.
Famine cycles are natural and recurrent even under great rulers.
Famine and abundance are Heaven's recurrent course; Yu and Tang experienced them too.
Chinese 禹、湯被之矣 names Yu and Tang; replacing them with vague 'great rulers' omits the explicit persons, and the proposed sentence restores both names and Heaven's course accurately.
Historical resilience came from pre-positioned reserves, not crisis improvisation.

Thus Yao and Yu endured nine years of floods, and Tang seven years of drought, yet no one in their states was abandoned to starve, because their reserves were ample and their preparations made in advance.

The original drops the exemplum entirely. This revision restores Yao, Yu, Tang, the disasters, and the advance reserves while rendering 國亡捐瘠者 as natural English rather than 'no abandoned emaciated people.'
Given favorable baseline conditions, weak reserves indicate policy failure rather than natural destiny.
Now with the realm unified, land and population no less than under Tang or Yu, and without multi-year flood or drought, why have accumulations still not reached their level?
Chinese 不避湯、禹 explicitly compares land and population to Tang and Yu; the idiomatic paraphrase erases that comparison, and the proposed wording restores it naturally.
Emperor Wen implemented a tiered grain-to-rank schedule with escalating thresholds for higher titles.
Emperor Wen then followed Cuo's advice and ordered the people to submit grain to the frontiers under a tiered grain-to-rank schedule with escalating thresholds for higher titles.
Chinese 文帝從錯之言 attributes the frontier grain-for-rank order to following Cuo's counsel; omitting that attribution is a real error the proposal corrects.
Later policy partially restored tax at a light one-thirtieth rate.
Thirteen years later, in the second year of Emperor Jing, the people were ordered to pay half the field rent, a tax of one in thirty.
Chinese 後十三歲，孝景二年 names the interval and Emperor Jing's second year for restoring half field rent at one-thirtieth; 'later policy' erases those facts, and the proposed wording is accurate.
Roughly seven decades of relative stability produced broad fiscal abundance and full granaries.
For about seventy years down to the start of Emperor Wu's reign, relative stability produced broad fiscal abundance and full granaries.
Chinese 至武帝之初七十年間 anchors the seventy years at the start of Emperor Wu's reign; omitting 武帝 is a real gap the proposal restores without distortion.
Some tilled powerful households' fields and were taxed at fifteen of ten.
Some tilled powerful households' fields and were taxed at five parts in ten.
見稅什五 means a tax of five parts in ten (half), not 'fifteen of ten'; the proposed literal correction is exact.
The gloss lemma is 刭, romanized Jing, not Qin; the proposed literal fix corrects the false name while keeping the gloss sense 附根也.

Now Shouchang wants nearby purchase and to stop transport to inside passes, building warehouses and repairing ships, costing over two hundred million; with mobilizing crowds, I fear producing drought qi and people suffering disaster.

Now Shouchang wants to buy grain nearby and ship it by water into the passes, building granaries and repairing boats at a cost of more than two hundred million cash. Such a mobilization of labor, I fear, will generate drought qi and bring disaster upon the people.
In 近糴漕關內之穀, 漕 is grain transport by water, not 'stop.' This revision restores the direction into the passes and clarifies the costs, labor mobilization, and feared consequence.
He warned that large infrastructure and mobilization costs could trigger social and climatic harm.

He warned that Shouchang's plan to buy grain nearby and ship it into the passes would require granaries, boats, more than two hundred million cash, and mass labor, potentially provoking drought and disaster for the people.

The original drops the concrete policy. This revision restores nearby purchase, water transport into the passes, granaries, boats, the stated cost, mass labor, and the feared drought without the proposal's vague 'canal logistics.'
Agrarian advocacy also advanced other officials such as Cai Kui into major posts.
Agrarian advocacy also advanced other officials such as Cai Gui into major posts.
蔡癸 has given name 癸 (Gui); Kui is a false romanization, and replacing Cai Kui with Cai Gui corrects the naming error.
And Cai Kui, by loving agriculture, was sent to encourage commanderies and states, rising to high office.
And Cai Gui, by loving agriculture, was sent to encourage commanderies and states, rising to high office.
The same unit's literal likewise misreads 癸 as Kui; Gui is the correct given-name reading, and the rest of the sentence is already accurate.
